claims.claim: Art is the achievement of expression that gives a Secondary World the inner consistency of reality; consistency, not novelty, is what earns belief.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories' (full text, coolcalvary PDF)
claims.quote: the inner consistency of reality

claims.feature: Secondary Belief vs suspension of disbelief
claims.claim: Inside a successful Secondary World what is related is 'true' by that world's own laws, and the instant a reader's disbelief arises the art has failed — suspension of disbelief is only a substitute for genuine Secondary Belief.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken

claims.claim: Fantasy's native advantage is arresting strangeness, which must be married to consistency or it decays into the merely fanciful and decorative.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: arresting strangeness

claims.claim: The more the images depart from the Primary World the harder inner consistency is to produce, so fantastic material demands more labour than sober material, not less.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material

claims.claim: Anyone can say 'the green sun'; building a world in which it commands Secondary Belief requires labour, thought and a special elvish craft — narrative art in its most potent mode.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: a kind of elvish craft

claims.claim: The adjective is the root spell of Faërie: to take green from grass or red from blood is already an enchanter's power, so fantasy is built at the level of the word.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: a part of speech in a mythical grammar

claims.claim: Fantasy's function of Recovery is regaining a clear view, freeing familiar things from the triteness of appropriation — the prose must make the known strange again.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: the drab blur of triteness or familiarity

claims.feature: fantasy belongs to words, not pictures or drama
claims.claim: Fantasy is best left to words because painting makes the fantastic technically too easy and Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy — the verbal medium is the proper one.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: Fantasy is a thing best left to words

claims.claim: Faërie is indescribable though not imperceptible; the writer gives glimpses rather than definitions, and analysis will not discover the secret of the whole.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: cannot be caught in a net of words

claims.claim: The association of fairy-stories with children is a historical accident, so the register must not be pitched down to a nursery audience.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: an accident of our domestic history

claims.claim: The fairy-story's true form is the sudden joyous turn that denies universal defeat without denying sorrow, so the prose must carry grief and joy in one register.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'On Fairy-stories'
claims.quote: poignant as grief

claims.claim: A fairy-story must be presented as true and cannot tolerate any frame or machinery suggesting the whole is a figment or illusion.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Fairy-Stories'
claims.quote: presented as 'true'

claims.claim: The instinct of linguistic invention is the fitting of notion to oral symbol and pleasure in contemplating the relation — words must sound like what they mean.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice' (full text, gwern PDF)
claims.quote: the fitting of notion to oral symbol

claims.claim: Pleasure in articulate sound and its symbolic use is independent of communication though entangled with it, and must never be forgotten in language-making.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: pleasure in articulate sound

claims.claim: An invented language with individual flavour must have a mythology woven into it, and conversely language construction will breed a mythology — names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: your language construction will breed a mythology

claims.claim: Tolkien's chief interest is word-form in itself and word-form in relation to meaning, the so-called phonetic fitness.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: word-form in relation to meaning

claims.feature: verse as the test of an invented language
claims.claim: The final fruition of an invented language is verse, which both expresses and fixes the maker's personal taste in sound.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: this final fruition: verse

claims.claim: In modern poetry word-form is seldom consciously marked and its effects are miscalled 'authentic magic'; Tolkien wants sound-pattern deliberately constructed to give pleasure.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: the word-form is seldom consciously marked

claims.claim: Word-form even unassociated with notions can give a perception of beauty; Greek, Finnish and Welsh are named as languages with characteristically beautiful word-form.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice'
claims.quote: capable of giving pleasure - a perception of beauty

claims.feature: association of form and sense (cellar door)
claims.claim: 'Cellar door' is beautiful dissociated from its sense, and the higher pleasure lies in words where form and sense associate — a phonaesthetic test the prose can be held to.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh')
claims.quote: the association of form and sense

claims.claim: Linguistic taste is partly inborn (the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue), so a writer's phonaesthetic choices express inherent predilections rather than fashion.
claims.source: Anna Smol, 'Tolkien's cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh' pp.190-1)
claims.quote: inherent linguistic predilections

claims.feature: illusion of historical truth and perspective
claims.claim: The illusion of historical truth and perspective in Beowulf is largely a product of art — an instinctive historical sense used with a poetical, not historical, object.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' (full text PDF)
claims.quote: largely a product of art

claims.claim: The impression of depth is the effect and justification of episodes and allusions to old tales that are darker and more desperate than the foreground — the background must be grimmer than the story.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: mostly darker, more pagan, and desperate than the foreground

claims.claim: Old stones (sources) exist to build the tower from whose top one sees the sea; the work is art, not a quarry, and its sources must not be dug for at the tower's expense.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: look out upon the sea

claims.claim: The poem's structure is a balance, an opposition of ends and beginnings (youth against age), not a steadily advancing narrative.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: an opposition of ends and beginnings

claims.claim: Old English lines are founded on a balance of two opposed halves, more like masonry than music, and the whole is a composition not a tune.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: more like masonry than music

claims.claim: Beowulf is not an epic but an heroic-elegiac poem whose first 3,136 lines are the prelude to a dirge — the elegiac is the governing tone.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: the prelude to a dirge

claims.feature: late, antiquarian voice (echo of an echo)
claims.claim: The poem is late not primitive: its maker told of things already old and weighted with regret, producing sorrows both poignant and remote.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: an echo of an echo

claims.claim: A translation must avoid colloquialism and false modernity and be literary and traditional, because the original's diction was poetical, archaic and artificial in its own day.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: colloquialism and false modernity

claims.claim: The language should be intentionally antiquated but not arcane — words still in literary use among educated people — avoiding both the colloquial and the obscure.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell (DBU), outline of 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: avoid both the colloquial and the obscure

claims.claim: The translator owes allegiance to the original's meaning and style and renders it into modern literary English, not present-day colloquial English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, J.R.R. Tolkien 'Thoughts on Translation (Beowulf)'
claims.quote: modern literary, not present-day colloquial

claims.claim: Resolving Old English compounds into phrases keeps colour but loosens and weakens the texture; compact naming is preferred.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: loosens and weakens the texture

claims.claim: Publishing The Hobbit under the convention that fairy-stories are for children had unfortunate effects on its mode of expression and narrative method, which he would have corrected if not rushed.
claims.source: Carpenter (ed.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215 to Walter Allen (April 1959, unsent draft)
claims.quote: unfortunate effects on the mode of expression and narrative method

claims.claim: Intelligent children of good taste single out the points in manner where the address is to children as blemishes.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 215'
claims.quote: singled out the places where the address was to children

claims.feature: whimsy to historical (register arc of The Hobbit)
claims.claim: The Hobbit begins in a whimsy, even facetious, mode and moves steadily to a more serious, consistent and historical one — and he regrets much of the early manner.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215
claims.quote: more consistent and historical

claims.feature: LotR addressed to no class of reader
claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings was not specially addressed to children or any other class but to anyone who enjoys a long exciting story; adult language is assumed.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215
claims.quote: a long exciting story

claims.claim: In so far as The Hobbit was dressed up as for children in style or manner, Tolkien regrets it, and so, he says, do the children.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165 to Houghton Mifflin (June 1955)
claims.quote: in style or manner, I regret it

claims.claim: Words like plenilune and argent are beautiful before they are understood; limiting vocabulary to a child's supposed reach cuts off the gifted from extending it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234 to Jane Neave (22 Nov 1961)
claims.quote: beautiful words before they are understood

claims.feature: first meeting in a living context
claims.claim: A fine word should first be met in a living context, not a dictionary; 'argent' does not mean 'silver' because its phonetic incarnation and heraldic overtones differ.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234
claims.quote: in a living context, and not in a dictionary

claims.claim: Tolkien deprecated the writing-down, flattening attitude that leaves children with little respect and no love for words; The Hobbit's early part was his one such mistake.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 234'
claims.quote: writing down, flattening attitude

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings is meant to include, even in style, the colloquialism and vulgarity of hobbits, poetry, and the highest style of prose.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131 to Milton Waldman (1951)
claims.quote: the colloquialism and vulgarity of Hobbits

claims.feature: tone rises with the hero's development
claims.claim: In The Hobbit the tone and style change with the hobbit's development, passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high and relapsing on the return.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131
claims.quote: passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high

claims.claim: The legendarium ranges from the cosmogonic to the fairy-story level, the larger founded on the lesser and the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Letter 131)
claims.quote: the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths

claims.claim: Westron is equated with English and everything in it translated with differentiation of style for dialect; related tongues become English-related forms (Rohan like Old English, Dale Scandinavian); alien tongues are left alone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144 to Naomi Mitchison (25 Apr 1954)
claims.quote: some differentiation of style to represent dialectal differences

claims.claim: In Gondor the Common Speech is spoken in a nobler and more antique style, which the Elves also adopt when they use it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: nobler and rather more antique style

claims.claim: As a story it is good that many things stay unexplained (especially if an explanation exists); Tolkien fears he erred by explaining too much, and readers stuck at the Council of Elrond.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: a lot of things unexplained

claims.claim: Quenya is built on a Latin basis with Finnish and Greek because they give him phonaesthetic pleasure; Sindarin is devised to resemble British-Welsh because that character fits Celtic-type legends.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: give me ‘phonaesthetic’ pleasure

claims.claim: The invention of languages is the foundation, the stories were made to provide a world for the languages, a name comes first and the story follows, and the book is largely an essay in linguistic aesthetic.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
claims.quote: largely an essay in ‘linguistic aesthetic’

claims.claim: Only as much 'language' was left in The Lord of the Rings as readers could be expected to stomach — the visible Elvish is a deliberate restraint.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
claims.quote: as I thought would be stomached by readers

claims.claim: The sensibility to linguistic pattern affects Tolkien emotionally like colour or music; Gothic taught him aesthetic pleasure in a language for its own sake.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163 to W.H. Auden (7 Jun 1955)
claims.quote: affects me emotionally like colour or music

claims.claim: A tale of this sort must consult the writer's roots: a man of the North-west sets it in a world with the Shoreless Sea to the West and endless enemy lands to the East.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163
claims.quote: consult your roots

claims.claim: Tushery is bogus medieval stuff coloured with expletives like tush, pish, zounds; real archaic English is far terser than modern and says things the slack modern idiom cannot.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171 to Hugh Brogan (Sept 1955, unsent draft)
claims.quote: far more terse than modern

claims.claim: Putting Théoden's thought into modern idiom would be an insincerity, a disunion of word and meaning, because people who think like that do not talk a modern idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Narrative (not only dialogue) archaism is defended because heroic scenes do not occur in a modern setting; changing the idiom would be like changing helms and hauberks into modern uniforms.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: helms, shields, hauberks into modern uniforms

claims.claim: 'Helms too they chose' puts the emphasised word in prominent first place without a clutter of empty words, a trick modern English should relearn by example.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a lot of little ‘empty’ words

claims.claim: English's wealth leaves a choice of styles without any risk of unintelligibility, and refusing to use it is a parochialism of time.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a choice of styles

claims.feature: Elrond's archaism by grammar and vocabulary
claims.claim: The Gateway summary of the Brogan draft records Tolkien rejecting 'tushery' as applying only to low-quality pastiche rather than real archaic English, with the Théoden passage as his sample.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 171'
claims.quote: slack and often frivolous idiom

claims.feature: legends and language share a taste
claims.claim: Legends depend on the language they belong to and a living language on its legends; Esperanto is dead for lack of legends, and Tolkien's legends were invented to match his languages' taste.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 180 to 'Mr Thompson' (14 Jan 1956)
claims.quote: legends of the same ‘taste’

claims.feature: differentiation by diction and idiom, not accent
claims.claim: No vowel/consonant accent-marking is wanted; Orcs deliberately never drop aitches in the text; the linguistic differentiation Tolkien built is in diction and idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193 to Terence Tiller (2 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: in diction, idiom, and so on

claims.feature: Minas Tirith as the standard register
claims.claim: Minas Tirith is to the Common Speech as London is to modern English — the standard of comparison, whose people have no accent.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: as London is to modern English

claims.claim: The Rohirrim spoke with a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation than modern urbans, and in Common Speech speak the best Minas Tirith, perhaps a little too carefully as a learned tongue.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation

claims.feature: Orcs nasty by delivery not vulgarism
claims.claim: Orcs are to sound nasty through intonation, articulation and tempo, not through conventional features of modern vulgar English.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 193'
claims.quote: intonation, articulation, and tempo

claims.feature: reading, not drama (necklace on a thread)
claims.claim: The book needs the older art of the reading mime; dramatization flattens scenery and characters, whereas passages read as a necklace upon a thread of narration would be fairer.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 194 to Terence Tiller (6 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: as a necklace upon a thread of narration

claims.claim: The tale was conceived epically rather than dramatically, so dramatizing it without liberties strips setting from dialogue and leaves both flat.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 194'
claims.quote: a tale told epically

claims.feature: verse triggers archaic style; no modern rusticity
claims.claim: A speaker who breaks into formal verse uses an archaic style as anyone capable of verse then would; where dialect marked place not rank, avoid any modern rusticity.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 152 to Rayner Heppenstall (22 Sept 1954)
claims.quote: avoid any modern rusticity

claims.feature: miles are miles (literal geography and season)
claims.claim: Though a fairy-story, the tale takes place in this earth's northern hemisphere: miles, days and weather are literal, and seasons are pictorial and basic to the tone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210 to Forrest J. Ackerman (June 1958)
claims.quote: miles are miles, days are days, and weather is weather

claims.feature: tone not to be lowered to childish fairy-tale
claims.claim: 'Old scamp!' exemplifies the treatment's tendency to lower the tone toward a childish fairy-tale; the setting is not fairy-land but real river-lands in autumn.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: in real river-lands in autumn

claims.feature: neither contes de fées nor scientification
claims.claim: Any pull toward French fairy-tale style or toward science-fiction diction ('food concentrate' for lembas) is alien to the story; both modes are rejected.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: Both modes are alien to my story

claims.feature: characters kept in style and sentiment
claims.claim: Speeches must represent the characters as written, in style and sentiment; perverting a character is resented more than spoiling plot or scenery.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: in style and sentiment

claims.claim: Anticipating later devices and assimilating one incident to another have a flattening effect; a scene of gloom and silence beats yet another scene of screams and slashings.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: flattening the tale out

claims.claim: The Ringbearers' action and the heroic matter are totally different in tone and scenery and must each be kept in coherent sequence; jumbling destroys both.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: totally different in tone and scenery

claims.claim: Rohan is a dwelling of Men in a heroic age: no private chambers, the king receiving on the dais of his hall — details must fit the world described.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: a dwelling of Men in an ‘heroic age’

claims.claim: Gandalf must not splutter: despite humour and an avuncular manner he is a person of high and noble authority and great dignity.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 210'
claims.quote: Gandalf was to be spluttering. Tolkien disapproved

claims.feature: a world for the languages (personal aesthetic)
claims.claim: The long book was an attempt to create a world for languages that agreed with his personal aesthetic — a situation in which an Elvish greeting would be ordinary.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 205'
claims.quote: create a world for languages

claims.feature: glimpses of a large history; unattainable vistas
claims.claim: Part of the attraction is the glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant city in sunlit mist; to go there destroys the magic unless new unattainable vistas open.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 247 to Colonel Worskett (20 Sept 1963)
claims.quote: unless new unattainable vistas are again revealed

claims.feature: language requires a habitation and history
claims.claim: Anyone who carries language invention far discovers that a language requires a suitable habitation and a history in which it can develop — the origin of the imaginary histories.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 294 to the Plimmers (8 Feb 1967)
claims.quote: a suitable habitation, and a history

claims.claim: The nomenclature, built from pre-existing invented languages, achieves a verisimilitude that assists literary belief in the story as historical; name-meanings are relevant solely to the fiction.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297 drafts to 'Mr Rang' (Aug 1967)
claims.quote: the ‘literary belief in the story as historical

claims.feature: Anglo-Saxon as translation device for Rohan only
claims.claim: Anglo-Saxon is used for the Mark's names and glimpses of its speech purely as a device of translation, and is the sole field for those names — delusory anywhere else.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297
claims.quote: as a device of ‘translation’

claims.claim: Tolkien objected to translating personal nomenclature and insisted the word hobbit stay unaltered; the Shire is a parody of rural England whose toponymy is not Dutch.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Letter 190'
claims.quote: the word hobbit stayed unaltered

claims.claim: Shire names are not meaningless but English in form, built from elements now obsolete, dialectal, or worn-down and obscured.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings' (Nomenclature, full text)
claims.quote: obsolete or dialectal

claims.feature: euphonious names of familiar English style
claims.claim: Common-Speech renderings of Elvish names (Rivendell for Imladris) are made to be both a translation and a euphonious name of familiar English style.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: a euphonious name of familiar English style

claims.claim: Leaving such names untranslated would introduce an unexplained element with no place in the feigned linguistic history of the period — the nomenclature is a single designed scheme.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the feigned linguistic history of the period

claims.feature: hobbits adopt the style of those they meet
claims.claim: Appendix F explains varied hobbit speech by saying the more learned hobbits knew book-language and were quick to adopt the style of those they met.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (quoting Appendix F)
claims.quote: quick to note and adopt the style

claims.feature: Appendix F cut to a third
claims.claim: The published Appendix F is only about one-third as long as its draft F2 — the visible linguistic apparatus is a deliberate reduction.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'The Appendix on Languages'
claims.quote: only about one-third as long

claims.claim: Scholars summarise the depth effect as four techniques: enormous background scale, casual incomplete mentions, multiple accounts with apparent contradictions (Red Book frame), and varying literary styles.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: casual, incomplete mentions

claims.feature: editorial frame (last of the philological editors)
claims.claim: Tolkien positioned himself as the last of a line of philological editors of the Red Book, so the paratexts make the text seem annotated by many hands over ages.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories'
claims.quote: the last of a line of philological editors

claims.claim: In the Valedictory Address Tolkien says he would rather wring the juice out of a single sentence or explore one word than survey — the sentence-level craft is the method.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey on 'The Monsters and the Critics and other essays'
claims.quote: wring the juice out of a single sentence

claims.claim: Tolkien singularised the speech of important characters to show social and cultural differences and asked why one should refuse to use the wealth of English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Ferré, Lauzon and Riggs, 'Translating Tolkien'
claims.quote: refuse to use the wealth of English

claims.claim: To give a language individual flavour it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Carl Hostetter, 'Tolkien's Invented Languages'
claims.quote: the threads of an individual mythology

claims.claim: The incarnate mind, the tongue and the tale are coeval; sub-creation is a birthright because we make as we are made.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Verlyn Flieger, 'On Fairy Stories'
claims.quote: We make, because we are made

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings shows far more deliberate stylistic variation than any other novel, with sixty poems and songs in many styles and several languages.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey, 'The Lord of the Rings, Book of the Century'
claims.quote: far more deliberate stylistic variation

claims.claim: A reader's essay argues Elrond's age is implied by archaic word order and that each character's speech stays consistent throughout, conveying culture and rank.
claims.source: K.G., 'To Make a Soul: Tolkien and Variations of Speech' (tolkienmedievalandmodern blog)
claims.quote: Elrond's age and sagacity implied through archaic word order

claims.claim: Moorcock holds that high fantasy's prose is the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe, and that this is the predominant tone of The Lord of the Rings — the direct counter to Tolkien's claim to have shed the children's manner.
claims.source: Michael Moorcock, 'Epic Pooh' (1978; revolutionsf copy via Wayback)
claims.quote: the prose of the nursery-room

claims.claim: Bratman and Williams reject Moorcock's reading of the prose as out of context and uninformed.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Epic Pooh'
claims.quote: one wonders what book Moorcock read
